subject: system-design
title: Load Balancers
summary: The component that spreads incoming requests across a pool of servers. It is what actually makes horizontal scaling and zero-downtime deploys possible.

blocks.text: A load balancer sits in front of a pool of servers and distributes incoming requests across them. To the client it looks like a single endpoint; behind it, the work is shared by many machines. This one component is what lets you scale out instead of up.

blocks.caption: One endpoint to the client; the load balancer fans requests out across the server pool.

blocks.text: Load balancers operate at one of two layers. An L4 (transport) balancer routes on IP and port without looking inside the request, so it is fast and protocol-agnostic. An L7 (application) balancer reads the HTTP request, so it can route by path, header, or cookie, terminate TLS, and make smarter decisions at the cost of a little more work.

items: Round robin: hand each request to the next server in turn.
Weighted: send more traffic to bigger or healthier nodes.
Least connections: pick the server with the fewest active requests.
IP or consistent hashing: map a key to a server so the same client lands on the same node.

blocks.text: The balancer continually probes each server and routes only to the ones that pass. When a node stops responding it's pulled from the pool, and traffic shifts to the survivors automatically. This is also what makes rolling deploys safe: drain a node, update it, return it to rotation, repeat.
Health checks plus a server pool are what enable horizontal scaling and zero-downtime rolling deploys. You can add capacity or swap versions without the client ever noticing.

Local load balancing spreads traffic within a single data center. Global load balancing (GSLB, often via DNS) steers users to the right region first, whether nearest, fastest, or healthiest. Then a local balancer takes over inside that region. Real systems usually run both layers together.

Sticky sessions pin a user to one server so that server's in-memory state stays valid. It works, but it unbalances the pool and breaks when that node dies. The cleaner answer is stateless servers: keep session state in a shared store so any server can handle any request, and the balancer is free to send traffic anywhere.

blocks.title: Don't make the balancer the single point of failure
blocks.text: If everything flows through one load balancer, the balancer itself is now the weak link. Run a redundant pair, active-passive or active-active, so losing one doesn't take the whole system down.
